title: Commitment Corridor: Q4 allocation framework for Hosted API + Model Catalog
creator: Aisha Moreno
description:
Problem: As usage of Hosted API grows and we expand the model catalog, product, infra, and sales teams need a lightweight but prescriptive commitment policy that ties quarterly capacity allocations to OKRs and provides clear contingency ribs for surges. Current playbooks are fragmented across docs and teams (runways, hedges, canary windows) and teams repeatedly ask for a single frame-of-decision for Q4 commitments.

Goal: Deliver the "Commitment Corridor" — a one-page framework and associated handoff checklist that standardizes how we translate OKR-driven demand forecasts into committed Dedicated capacity, hosted runway guardrails, canary windows, and model-catalog rotation windows for the coming quarter. The corridor should make trade-offs explicit (cost vs availability vs model freshness) and provide a simple escalation path when forecasts exceed the corridor.

Scope: Hosted API and Model Catalog commit decision-making for Q4. Includes definition of corridor bands (Base, Buffer, Surge), mapping to OKR priority tiers, guidance for quantization/kv-cache trade-offs, and a templated ticket/PR checklist for coordination between PM / Eng / SRE / Sales. Does not include low-level autoscaler implementation (handled in ENG backlog) but includes precise requirements and hedging numbers for them.
acceptance_criteria:
1) One-page Commitment Corridor doc reviewed and signed off by product leads and infra SREs.
2) Handoff checklist (concrete steps and owners) published in Confluence and linked in quarterly planning.
3) Two simulated scenarios (15% and 60% demand delta) with recommended actions and cost estimates produced and validated by MLE and Infra.
4) Canary & rollback windows defined for model rotations with clear gate metrics.
5) OKR traceability: each committed lane maps to at least one top-level OKR and is visible in roadmap tool.
notes_updates: 2025-01-12 Kickoff: Align PM, Eng, SRE. Captured initial constraints: Dedicated pool purchase lead time (3 weeks), hosted capacity burst limits, model onboarding effort (2-3 engineer-weeks per major model).
2025-01-18 Draft corridor bands created (Base 0-40%, Buffer 40-70%, Surge 70-100%). Shared with infra for feasibility feedback.

2025-01-21 Infra feedback: Buffer band should be defined by commitable GPU-hours and a recommended autoscaler profile. Action: ENG to run capacity runbook simulation (ENG-4123) and return numbers by 2025-01-30.

2025-01-28 PM review: Replaced generic 'surge' actions with explicit rollback knobs (model variant fallback, reduce batch size, enable kv-cache prioritization). Added cost delta estimates for each action.
2025-02-03 Design review: Added a visual corridor diagram and simplified decision flow. Design pointed out potential cognitive load; we pared down to 3 decision nodes.
Future: Schedule tabletop walkthrough with Sales and Customer Success to validate contract hedging language (target before 2025-02-20).
rollout_plan: 1) Finalize corridor bands and numeric hedges after ENG capacity sim. 2) Publish Confluence doc + checklist. 3) Run two scenario simulations and publish results to roadmap channel. 4) Include corridor in Q4 planning ritual; require signoff for any committed capacity outside Base band. 5) Execute tabletop walkthrough with CS/Sales to validate commercial messaging. 6) Lock release: add corridor slug to quarterly kickoff and annotate release notes (catalog-2025.04).
metrics: Committed capacity accuracy vs realized usage (target <15% variance)
Canary model degradation incidents post-rotation (target 0 major incidents)
Time from surge detection to remediation decision (target <30min)
Cost delta of executed surge actions (tracked in console by route/model)
Percent of OKRs with assigned committed lanes (target 100%)
risks: Over-committing reserved capacity increases fixed costs if forecasts are wrong.
Underestimating model onboarding effort could block rotation windows and degrade freshness.
Cross-team misalignment (Sales promises vs commitment corridor) could lead to customer SLA violations.
Incomplete autoscaler instrumentation may prevent recommended surge actions from being executed reliably.
